taxonomic_note: Species-level learner concept, distinct from the other Elymus species in this batch. Hybrids and infraspecific variants can blur characters; use an intact mature spikelet and do not force a hybrid/intermediate into either species.
look_here_first: CANADA WILDRYE (*Elymus canadensis*): follow a maturing nodding, unbranched awned SPIKE; original Harms I/i1 show green/ripe heads. In J/J1 see the central RACHIS joints carrying two or more multi-flowered units with long DIVERGING AWNS; J3 shows real exserted ANTHERS. Compare the separate detached S spikelet with original d disarticulation (true outer GLUMES versus individual inner LEMMAS/PALEAS), not just a fuzzy silhouette. Harms L shows actual clasping AURICLES and short true membranous LIGULE; these are genus clues, not the Canada-Virginia split. That split requires narrow straighter V-shaped basal glumes versus pale hardened outbowed U feet on multiple mature SAME SOURCE nodes; variable forms and documented hybrids mean contradictory specimens remain Elymus sp. Full Texas rooted crown/independent county voucher and exact measured glume-base macro still need more evidence.

project_inclusion.learner_admission_basis: Calvin-approved Master Plant Pool (Elymus canadensis: 3 source flags; Elymus virginicus: 2) and existing canonical Elymus genus comparison lesson
project_inclusion.range_basis: No BONAP/NAPA-first three-target-county audit completed for this curation batch. Source-pool admission is independent of range certification; no native metrics credit.

best_field_traits: 1 · MATURE SPIKE: follow full top of stem. A usually long (~8–20 cm) terminal unbranched spike often bends or DROOPS at maturity; not a loose branching PANICLE.
2 · LONG AWNS: lemma awns spread/curve outward (commonly 15–40 mm); seedhead looks shaggy as it ripens.
3 · NODE: two or sometimes more multiflowered spikelets attach at one central rachis joint; narrow pointed glumes typically have relatively straight V-like bases.
4 · COLLAR: leaf blade sheaths with small clasping AURICLES and membranous LIGULE; common Elymus characteristics, NOT a species separator.
5 · Texas A&M warns of CANADA × VIRGINIA hybridization and variable forms. If nodding/posture and glume shapes conflict, label Elymus sp. and collect a mature intact voucher.
6 · Against Texas wintergrass: cool-season is shared, but wintergrass has a loose branching panicle with individually one-flowered spikelets and single hard sharp-callused awned fruits.
morphology_keys.comparison_training: Versus E. virginicus: usually a more nodding, open/shaggy mature spike, longer divergent awns and glumes with straighter V-like bases. E. virginicus generally retains an erect tighter spike, shorter straighter awns and hardened outward-bowed U-like glume bases. Hybrids and variable forms occur; require several intact spikelets.
morphology_keys.glume_base: The outer bracts (glumes) are narrow, linear and often nearly straight at their attachment to the central rachis node, less obviously outward-curved and bony than Virginia wildrye. Check on several fully mature spikelets from the SAME plant; damaged, immature, or hybrid heads may conflict.
photo_diagnostic_second_pass_20261022: 1. Trace a REAL attached upper culm/flag leaf into a SINGLE terminal unbranched SPIKE, Harms b and I. Don't infer roots from the cropped upper culm image.
2. Compare the young flowering I head with mature i1 DRYING heads: ripening awns diverge and the whole head often bends/nods. Not every arched head is Canada, and head position alone is unreliable.

3. Open the central RACHIS on J1: at each joint identify TWO OR MORE actual multi-flowered SPIKELETS, not each long awn as a separate spikelet. Compare with Hordeum generally 3 one-flowered spikelets/node.
4. J and J3 show genuine yellowish ANTHERS dangling during anthesis. These are real pollen-bearing organs, not glumes, awns, stigmas or seeds.
5. S isolates ONE spikelet from the spike and shows two basal narrow GLUMES plus a series of inner awned floret lemmas; no additional microscopic labels unless actual pixel verified.

6. The 'd' image demonstrates mature DISARTICULATION: rachis node, detached glumes, florets/rachilla segments. Study what sheds and where it attaches before labeling complete spikelets versus single florets.

7. L shows the true blade–sheath collar. On an attached leaf inspect the hooked lateral AURICLES and short central membranous LIGULE, an important genus clue; these are not species-separating on their own.

8. Compare Canada source-labeled straighter narrow V glume bases with actual other-species Virginia photograph showing shorter hardened OUTWARD-U-CURVED glume feet; use several attached mature nodes from same identified plants and real mm reference.

9. Count real lookalikes: Texas wintergrass has a BRANCHED panicle of single-flowered hard fruits; foxtail barley often 3 one-flowered spikelets/node. Variation or Canada×Virginia hybridization: leave Elymus sp. rather than guess.

10. Final teach-back requires an independently identified, legal Hays/nearby SAME rooted tuft, intact nodding spike, collar and multiple mature glume bases with 1mm scale; image-by-image mobile arrows must be inspected before FINISHED.

comparisons.key_distinctions: Versus E. virginicus: usually a more nodding, open/shaggy mature spike, longer divergent awns and glumes with straighter V-like bases. E. virginicus generally retains an erect tighter spike, shorter straighter awns and hardened outward-bowed U-like glume bases. Hybrids and variable forms occur; require several intact spikelets.

field_matrix.where_to_look: Compare several mature attached rachis nodes from each species; photograph overall seed-spike profile too.
field_matrix.this_species: CANADA: head usually NODS, longer spreading CURVED awns, glume bases slender and comparatively STRAIGHT/V-shaped.
field_matrix.look_alike: VIRGINIA: head usually ERECT and densely packed, awns shorter/straighter, glume feet pale thickened and outward U-BOWED.
field_matrix.quick_rule: Nodding + long spread awns + straight narrow glume feet → Canada candidate. Upright + bowed bony U-feet → Virginia candidate. Hybrids: hold Elymus sp.

field_matrix.where_to_look: Determine spike vs branching PANICLE: look for continuous crowded rachis nodes with MULTIPLE florets in each spikelet.
field_matrix.this_species: CANADA has one terminal unbranched spike, with multi-flowered spikelets at successive rachis nodes, each with its own outer glumes and multiple lemma awns.
field_matrix.look_alike: Wintergrass has loose branching panicle of ONE-flowered hardened spikelets, each floret with ONE extremely long twisted awn and a sharp callus.
field_matrix.quick_rule: Multi-flowered spikelets along one central SPIKE = Elymus; isolated one-flowered grains along branching PANICLE = Nassella.

field_matrix.taxon: Barley or foxtail barley · Hordeum spp.
field_matrix.where_to_look: At one central rachis node check the number, shape and length of attached spikelets and whether multiple florets occur.
field_matrix.this_species: Elymus usually two (sometimes more) multi-FLOWERED spikelets per node, with relatively clear narrow glumes and awned lemmas.
field_matrix.look_alike: Hordeum often has distinct groups of 3 spikelets per rachis node, with very conspicuous long bristles and commonly ONE flower per spikelet.
field_matrix.quick_rule: A bristly whole head is not enough. Compare the cluster of spikelets/floret count on one attached node.

field_matrix.where_to_look: Inspect leaf auricles, actual glume basal width and spikelet floret number, then use regional dichotomous key.
field_matrix.this_species: Canada tends to long drooping heads; glumes narrow straight basal form.
field_matrix.look_alike: Elymus glaucus, other wildryes and Canada × Virginia intermediate crosses overlap in habit and awns.
field_matrix.quick_rule: Contradictory morphology → Elymus sp., do not force two-species classification.

not_reliable_alone: One nodding or upright head without mature glume bases — posture can change with drying, wind and variation.
Awn color, long-awn bristliness, panicle size or leaf blade width alone.
One damaged or immature spikelet without its intact lower glume bases.
A vegetative leaf/auricle photo; sufficient for Elymus genus orientation but not these species.
Assuming the Montana source-labelled photos constitute a Hays County voucher, or that both species have passed the separate target-zone native certification.

visual_comparison.title: Canada wildrye — real spikelet pairs, flowering anthers, disarticulation and clasping auricles
visual_comparison.subtitle: 11 real source-specific locally stored Canada wildrye JPEGs, including 9 credited copyrighted Bob Harms Central Texas macro originals + 2 Matt Lavin Commons images. 13 species teaching panels, including actual paired nodes/anthers/collar and Virginia glume-base comparison. Exact same-voucher mm anatomy still needed.
visual_comparison.memory_rule: CANADA WILDRYE: NODDING mature single SPIKE, LONG splayed AWNS, TWO OR MORE multi-FLORETED SPIKELETS per central rachis NODE, narrow STRAIGHTER basal GLUMES; tiny membranous LIGULE plus clasping AURICLES (genus clues). VIRGINIA = typically erect spike and bowed hardened U-shaped glume feet. Hybrids can overlap.

field_photo_quickcheck.heading: Canada wildrye — follow seed spike, then its paired glumes
steps: 1. Trace a REAL attached upper culm/flag leaf into a SINGLE terminal unbranched SPIKE, Harms b and I. Don't infer roots from the cropped upper culm image.
2. Compare the young flowering I head with mature i1 DRYING heads: ripening awns diverge and the whole head often bends/nods. Not every arched head is Canada, and head position alone is unreliable.

3. Open the central RACHIS on J1: at each joint identify TWO OR MORE actual multi-flowered SPIKELETS, not each long awn as a separate spikelet. Compare with Hordeum generally 3 one-flowered spikelets/node.
4. J and J3 show genuine yellowish ANTHERS dangling during anthesis. These are real pollen-bearing organs, not glumes, awns, stigmas or seeds.
5. S isolates ONE spikelet from the spike and shows two basal narrow GLUMES plus a series of inner awned floret lemmas; no additional microscopic labels unless actual pixel verified.

6. The 'd' image demonstrates mature DISARTICULATION: rachis node, detached glumes, florets/rachilla segments. Study what sheds and where it attaches before labeling complete spikelets versus single florets.

7. L shows the true blade–sheath collar. On an attached leaf inspect the hooked lateral AURICLES and short central membranous LIGULE, an important genus clue; these are not species-separating on their own.

8. Compare Canada source-labeled straighter narrow V glume bases with actual other-species Virginia photograph showing shorter hardened OUTWARD-U-CURVED glume feet; use several attached mature nodes from same identified plants and real mm reference.

9. Count real lookalikes: Texas wintergrass has a BRANCHED panicle of single-flowered hard fruits; foxtail barley often 3 one-flowered spikelets/node. Variation or Canada×Virginia hybridization: leave Elymus sp. rather than guess.

10. Final teach-back requires an independently identified, legal Hays/nearby SAME rooted tuft, intact nodding spike, collar and multiple mature glume bases with 1mm scale; image-by-image mobile arrows must be inspected before FINISHED.

measured_checks.spike: Usually approximately 8–20 cm, frequently arching or nodding at maturity.
measured_checks.lemma_awns: Often about 15–40 mm, spreading or curved.
measured_checks.glumes: Inspect and photograph narrow glume bases at several intact nodes; no measurement inferred from distant image.
measured_checks.ligule_collar: Small auricles and membranous ligule support Elymus but do not distinguish Canada from Virginia wildrye.
measured_checks.growth: Perennial cool-season grass; photograph crown, intact spike and several nodes.

lookalikes: Elymus virginicus: usually more upright and compact, with more bowed hardened glume bases; hybridization complicates IDs.
Hordeum spp.: often three one-flowered spikelets at a rachis node rather than paired multiflowered wildrye spikelets.
Nassella leucotricha: branching panicle with single-flowered spikelets and long twisted awns.
